s: require adaptation Natural conditions of existence require no artificial aids and should guide human life and government. Adapting to them prevents the eight forms of refinement from becoming hindrances and spoilers.

has natural goodness [which may be fatally forced down or stirred up] The human heart can be forced down or stirred up, and either treatment has a fatal issue. It may be softened by gentleness, but cutting and polishing it makes it unstable and uncontrollable.

The Mihists are one of five competing schools, arising beside the Confucianists amid rivalry, fraud, and coercive confusion. They preach charity, duty to one’s neighbour, and universal love, even amid cangues and fetters. Following Mih Tzŭ and Yü’s toil, they practise self-mortification and relentless work, but later divide into disputing groups that call one another schismatics.

possesses perfect TAO [as described by the Yellow Emperor] Kuang Ch'êng Tzŭ tells the Yellow Emperor that governing has disturbed heaven and earth and prevented perfect TAO. He teaches that stillness, purity, withdrawal from external knowledge, and preservation of the self lead to enduring life and harmony.

l: Spirit of the Clouds, Chuang Tzŭ
s: is_a power unavoidably summoned to govern [because people depend upon its movements] The Spirit of the Clouds worries that heaven and earth are out of harmony and seeks advice on nourishing living beings. The Vital Principle tells him that government is the source of the disorder and teaches him to feed the people with his heart, rest in inaction, and release intelligence.

Vital Principle teaches inaction and natural conditions so all things flourish, seeing government as disorder’s poison; he wanders without purpose, awaits events, and urges the Spirit of the Clouds to return.
All things arise through ONE, receive virtue, form, and nature, respond according to TAO, proceed naturally, and may return toward an original unconditioned state.

Confucius is presented as a Sage, scholar, teacher, student, Master of Tzŭ Kung, and member of the K'ung family. He devotes himself to loyalty, truth, charity, duty to one's neighbour, ceremonies, music, and distinguishing human relationships, while seeking success through long struggle and enduring four persecutions. He teaches that TAO existed before the universe and that there is no past, present, beginning, or end; he also values natural intelligence, internal constancy, unspoken language, and action without deeds. On traveling west to place his works in the Imperial library, he defends charity and duty as rooted in original nature, but Lao Tzŭ rejects this teaching. Surrounded at K'uang by men of Wei who mistake him for Yang Hu, he plays and sings without ceasing, remains fearless, and sees failure as fate and success as opportunity. He later tries unsuccessfully to reform Robber Chê, who denounces him as deceptive; Confucius departs shaken. At Apricot Altar, he follows and reveres an old fisherman, learning that attempts to reform and regulate others have drawn him from original purity. Finally, he is criticized as outwardly showy and specious, though the text attributes to him demanding tests of character and superior manhood.

Nothing recovers the Yellow Emperor's magic pearl after Intelligence, Sight, and Speech fail, showing spirituality through negation. One with Non-Existence, it is the Portal of God and the origin from which all things sprang; the Sage abides in its formless state.

Nature is an abiding inner principle enclosing the spiritual part. Cultivating it restores virtue and unconditioned fitness, while artificial will and fame should not erase what naturally abides, as horses and oxen having four feet exemplify.

l: the handover of the empire, Chuang Tzŭ
s: Resignation of the empire is repeatedly offered by Yao, Shun, and T'ang but is declined by people who prioritize preservation of life, inner virtue, or adherence to TAO. The refusals show that ruling is inferior to maintaining one's life and principles.
Chiang Lü Mien visits Chi Ch'ê, calls himself a fool, and seeks instruction after advising the Prince of Lu on decorum, thrift, loyalty, and impartiality.

teaches government of the Sage Chi Ch'ê criticizes Chiang Lü Mien's advice as ineffective and compares it to a mantis trying to stop a carriage. He explains that the government of the perfect Sage works by influencing people according to their natural dispositions, so that they become virtuous without being conscious of the influence.

l: the prince of Lu, Chuang Tzŭ
s: Prince of Lu rules Lu, asks Ch'ing about artistic mystery, then, melancholy over misfortune, is advised to renounce power and seek TAO inwardly.
An old gardener irrigates with a pitcher, rejects the well-sweep as corrupting, and rebukes Tzŭ Kung for seeking reputation and governing others without governing himself.

TÊ is a state of spiritual integrity: a perfect, harmonious, all-embracing virtue of spontaneity that abides in the natural. Perfect virtue belongs to the Sage, who remains passive and at repose, without sorrow, anxiety, attachment to distinctions, or injury to others; through natural influence such a person may govern without aggression. TÊ is glorified by Life, while TAO is its sovereign lord; spontaneous emotion is called passive virtue, and emotion not evoked externally is active virtue. It is injured by trifles, lost through love and hate, and obstructed by passion, artificial moral standards, fame, coercion, government, goodness, art, and learning. Once all-embracing and giving rise to charity, Virtue declines through historical ages as people are led from TAO and natural instinct. It is preserved by sincerity that responds to circumstances without aggression.

l: government of the Sage, Chuang Tzŭ
s: Government of the Sage follows natural disposition, aligns desires with virtue, confines officials to functions, employs ability, hears people, and achieves peace through responsive action.
travels_to ocean Chun Mang travels eastward to the ocean and tells Yüan Fêng how the Sage governs. He also describes the man of perfect virtue and the divine man.
meets Chun Mang [on the shore of the eastern sea] Yüan Fêng meets Chun Mang on the shore of the eastern sea and questions him about the ocean, the Sage, the man of perfect virtue, and the divine man.

is_damaged_by five senses [through sensory excess and likes and dislikes] Original nature is lost when the five colours, sounds, scents, tastes, and likes and dislikes overwhelm the senses and understanding. The text says that both highly honoured objects and despised conditions can involve destruction of original nature.
